aboutSections.title: What we make
aboutSections.body: PUZZLTHINK recreates games from brain-survival shows like The Devil's Plan and The Genius for the web. Starting with Wallgo from The Devil's Plan, we build the strategy games you wanted to try while watching — playable instantly in your browser with no install or sign-up.

aboutSections.title: WallGo
aboutSections.body: A strategy board game where you move a piece and then place a wall to divide the board. The player who claims the larger territory wins, and you can play against an AI opponent.

aboutSections.title: Sudoku
aboutSections.body: The classic logic puzzle: fill each row, column, and 3×3 box of a 9×9 grid with the digits 1 to 9 exactly once. Multiple difficulty levels and a notes mode are included.

aboutSections.title: How we operate
aboutSections.body: All games are free, and game records are stored only in your browser. Running costs may be covered by advertising revenue.

aboutSections.title: Who runs it
aboutSections.body: PUZZLTHINK is an independent project run by a solo developer. Send suggestions or bug reports to chlgnstj1@gmail.com.

aboutSections.title: Notice
aboutSections.body: PUZZLTHINK is an unofficial fan project and is not affiliated with The Devil's Plan, The Genius, or their broadcasters. Show names are used only to describe the games.

WallGoGuide.title: Wallgo Online — the Devil's Plan game, on the web
WallGoGuide.intro: Wallgo is a territory strategy game that became a fan favorite on Netflix's brain-survival show The Devil's Plan. If you enjoy shows like The Genius, it will feel right at home. PUZZLTHINK brings Wallgo to the web so anyone can play against two AI opponents right in the browser.
rules: On a 7×7 board, each player places 2 pieces in the order 1→2→3→3→2→1.
On your turn you have 90 seconds to move one piece 1 or 2 tiles in a straight line. You cannot pass through other pieces or walls, but you may move back the way you came.
After moving, you must build a wall on one open side of that piece. If time runs out, a wall is placed on a random side.
Once per game, each player may break through a wall on their movement path.
The game ends the moment every player is sealed off. The most tiles in the spaces containing your pieces wins; ties go to the largest single area.

faq.a: Right here on PUZZLTHINK — in any desktop or mobile browser, with no sign-up or install.

faq.q: Is it the same game as on The Devil's Plan?
faq.a: It is built on the core rules seen on the show — moving, building walls, and scoring territory — adapted for solo play against AI.
Yes. You can play a 3-player game against two AI opponents, or a 1:1 duel with 4 pieces each, like round 2 on the show. AI difficulty can be Easy, Normal, or Hard.

WallGoGuide.disclaimer: PUZZLTHINK is an unofficial fan project and is not affiliated with The Devil's Plan, The Genius, or their broadcasters. Show names are used only to describe the games.
duelRules: Each player starts with 4 pieces, 2 of which are already placed on fixed tiles.
A draw decides who goes first; the remaining 2 pieces are placed first→second→second→first.
Moving and wall building work as in the 3-player game, but there is no wall break.
The game ends when the two players are fully separated, and the larger territory wins.
WallGoGuide.strategyIntro: In Wallgo, opening placement and the position of a single wall can decide the game. Here are common situations drawn on the board. Columns are A–G and rows are 1–7 from the top.
legend: Side you could close but should leave

strategies.title: Anchor near a corner
strategies.body: Just as corners are easy to secure in Go, pieces near C3, E3, C5, or E5 can lock in territory with few walls. In a 3-player game, though, two opponents can close your two outer sides together and trap you in a few corner tiles, so keep an exit open.

strategies.title: The center D4 is stronger than it looks
strategies.body: Unlike a 19-line Go board, a 7×7 board brings fights to the center immediately. D4 can move two tiles in all four directions, giving the most mobility and a great spot to cut opponents’ expansion routes.

strategies.title: Never sit inside three walls
strategies.body: With walls on three sides, one more wall from an opponent leaves that piece unable to move. Unless you have a specific plan, never step into such a spot, and get out as soon as a third wall appears.

strategies.title: Two walls is risky in a 3-player game
strategies.body: With two opponents, a spot with two walls can be sealed in a single round, one wall each. Trapping one player helps the other two, so these team-ups happen naturally. If both opponents are nearby, avoid two-wall spots too.

strategies.title: Lock an opponent into a corner
strategies.body: Walls are not only for growing your own area. Trap an opponent in a few corner tiles and the rest of the board is split among everyone else, effectively removing them from the race for first. Move toward the spot that closes their last exit.

strategies.title: Do not close awkward territory for them
strategies.body: There is no need to seal an opponent’s narrow, hard-to-grow area. The game only ends when every space is split, so closing it just saves them turns. Left open, they must keep building walls inside the strip and shrink it themselves.

strategies.title: Block with your own pieces
strategies.body: No piece can move through another piece. In the 3-player game a wall can be broken once, but a path blocked by a piece cannot. Parking a piece in the middle of an opponent’s corridor is a more reliable block than a wall.

strategies.title: Wall break is all about timing
strategies.body: You only get one. Save it to flip the game at the end, or use it mid-game to cross into open space first and build momentum. Too late and the board is already decided; too early and you have nothing left in a crisis. An opponent about to close their region is a strong signal.
